title: What Is Frame Rate in Games? From 30 FPS to DLSS

scenes.title: What Is a Frame?
lines: When you choose 30 FPS or 60 FPS in a game's settings, what exactly are you changing?
In a game, a frame is the result of drawing the screen once: one image.
Freeze any movement and you will find a sequence of slightly different still images; this video follows that single image into game time, responsiveness, and modern graphics technology.

scenes.title: What 60 FPS Means
lines: FPS means frames per second: the frequency of frames processed or displayed in one second.
If the screen shows 60 images in one second, we call it 60 FPS.
In modern games, however, we sometimes need to distinguish directly rendered frames from the frames actually displayed.

scenes.title: Frames and Game Time
lines: Many early games moved a character a fixed distance whenever the screen advanced by one frame.
At frame zero, X is zero; on the next frame it is one, and then two.
A frame was both an image and a time marker, so a different refresh rate could also change movement, animation, and physics speed.

scenes.title: 30 FPS vs 60 FPS
lines: Imagine the same character moving the same distance during the same one second.
At 30 FPS there are 30 position samples, while at 60 FPS there are 60, including more positions in between.
The destination and travel time are unchanged, but smaller steps let a higher frame rate show the same time more densely and smoothly.

scenes.title: The Frame Budget
lines: Why not simply make every game run at the highest possible frame rate?
At 30 FPS a frame has about 33.33 milliseconds; at 60 it has 16.67, and at 120 it has 8.33.
The higher the frame rate, the smaller the time budget for physics, animation, game logic, and rendering.

scenes.title: Variable Frame Rate
lines: When more enemies, lights, and effects prevent the work from finishing on time, a reading of 60 can fall to 50 or 40.
Uneven intervals can feel rough even when average FPS is high, so we also need to inspect frame time: how long each image takes to make.

scenes.title: deltaTime
lines: Modern games often keep game time advancing at the same speed even when the display frame rate changes.
A common method is delta time: multiply speed by the real time elapsed during a frame.
Then 30-frame and 60-frame updates can reach the same position after the same one second.
Collision and physics may instead use a fixed time step for stability; the key is not to treat display frequency and game-time calculation as automatically identical.

scenes.title: 120 FPS and Monitor Hz
lines: PC games can also run at 120 or even 240 FPS.
More intermediate frames can show fast motion in finer steps and provide more chances to draw the result of a new input sooner.
But FPS is the number of frames produced by the game, while hertz is the monitor's refresh frequency; they affect each other, but they are not the same concept.

scenes.title: NTSC and PAL
lines: Older console games were strongly affected by regional television standards.
NTSC regions such as Japan and North America used about 60 fields, while PAL regions in Europe and Australia used 50.
If game logic was tied to refresh and left uncorrected, it could run at the 50-to-60 ratio; that was the cost of using frames directly as time.

scenes.title: Graphics Modes in the PS5 Era
lines: Many modern console games offer a choice between image quality and frame rate on the same hardware.
On PlayStation 5, resolution or quality modes generally favor higher image quality and complex effects, while performance modes favor a higher target frame rate.
Exact resolutions and targets vary by game, so quality is not always 30 and performance is not always 60.

scenes.title: What the GPU Does Per Frame
lines: A frame can include geometry, lighting, shadows, reflections, ray tracing, and post-processing.
The frame budget does not grow when effects are added, so the quality-versus-frame-rate tradeoff is a decision about where to spend limited milliseconds.

scenes.title: RTX 50 Series and Modern Rendering
lines: Graphics cards such as the RTX 50 Series include hardware for ray tracing and AI computation, expanding the range of complex lighting that can run in real time.
Modern rendering can also reconstruct a final screen from less computation instead of calculating every pixel and every frame entirely through traditional rendering.

scenes.title: The Pixel Cost of 4K
lines: A 4K image contains about 8.29 million pixels, and ray tracing can require multiple ray samples and additional work.
As resolution and lighting costs rise, must every final pixel always be calculated directly at 4K from the beginning?

scenes.title: DLSS Super Resolution
lines: DLSS Super Resolution renders below the target output resolution and then constructs a higher-resolution image.
It is not simple enlargement: it uses multiple lower-resolution frames, motion vectors, and information from previous frames.
The goal is to reduce directly calculated pixels while restoring detail close to the output resolution.
This reconstructs pixels, which is a different job from Frame Generation creating a new image.

scenes.title: Frame Generation
lines: Frame Generation analyzes motion between two directly rendered frames and generates a new image between them.
On the timeline, directly rendered frames are blue and generated frames are purple.
Placing generated frames between rendered ones can increase displayed frame count and motion smoothness.
But a generated frame is not a new simulation of the game world, so base render speed and input latency do not improve by the same ratio.

scenes.title: DLSS 4 Multi Frame Generation
lines: DLSS 4 introduced Multi Frame Generation on the RTX 50 Series.
At launch, it could generate up to three additional frames for each directly rendered frame.
DLSS 4.5 later expanded this direction with dynamic adjustment and support for more generated frames.
Actual results depend on game support, base render rate, resolution, GPU, and CPU conditions.

scenes.title: Rendered FPS vs Displayed FPS
lines: Generated frames between directly rendered frames can raise the displayed number, but not every image comes from a new input and simulation step.
That is why Rendered FPS and Displayed FPS should be reported separately when interpreting Frame Generation.

scenes.title: Why One FPS Number Is Not Enough
lines: Input passes through game simulation and rendering, then optionally upscaling and Frame Generation, before appearing on a monitor.
Rendered FPS is the direct rendering frequency, Displayed FPS includes generated frames, and input latency is the time from a button press to visible light.
Technologies such as NVIDIA Reflex can reduce system latency, but they do not merge these concepts into one.
So inspect base render rate, frame time, presentation method, and latency instead of relying on one large number.

scenes.title: Old and Modern Frame Pipelines
lines: In many simple older games, game logic, frame creation, and display output were closely tied in one line.
A modern game can separate input, simulation, rendering, upscaling, Frame Generation, and output, and those stages do not necessarily run at the same frequency.

scenes.title: Summary
lines: A frame is one screen image, and FPS is the frequency of frames processed or displayed in one second.
At 30, 60, and 120 FPS, the frame budgets are roughly 33, 16, and 8 milliseconds.
Delta time and fixed time steps help game-world time advance consistently when display frequency changes.
Modern rendering requires us to distinguish Super Resolution, directly rendered frames, generated frames, displayed frames, and input latency.
When building a game, choose a target frame rate, measure frame time, and verify that game speed remains the same across different performance levels.
